title: Artificial birth will change what it means to be human
subtitle: To be born in a machine
author: Anna M. Hennessey
introduction: Birth is an inseparable part of human experience — we were all born out of human bodies. Yet rapidly developing artificial womb technologies are on the cusp of replacing conventional birth, the social and political ramifications of which could be drastic. In this piece, Director of the Society for the Study of Pregnancy and Birth Anna Hennessey argues that these technologies have real potential to upend our social institutions, as well as our conceptions of gender, family and personhood — an understanding of the severity of this phenomenon involves realising the sublime and existential aspects of pregnancy and birth, not just their biological ones.
body:
Birth is the most foundational act of human experience; if we are not born, then there is no experience to be had. When most of us think about the act of birth, we imagine it happening in hospitals or sometimes homes—not in laboratories. Similarly, we usually think of women as the ones who give birth, though people who do not identify as women give birth too. In both cases, we imagine newborn infants emerging from female and human bodies.

Medical research groups and private companies have been developing advanced artificial wombs that are now on the cusp of supporting life before birth. These work in a way that goes beyond that of the historical infant incubator, known as an isolette, which has been used widely for decades in Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs) around the world. Although these artificial wombs cannot yet gestate life from conception to birth, we need to have the conversations now—before they are capable—about what it would mean for the human experience if they could.

Should such technologies develop to their full potential, we will need to renegotiate what it means to be born or give birth.

Arguments for why we need artificial womb technology primarily revolve around the issue of supporting premature babies. More speculative projects explore developing the technology further to support those who want children but cannot or do not want to go through childbirth, or to help countries in which the population is in decline. Most of us are already familiar with reproductive technologies such as in vitro fertilization (IVF) and modern infant incubators. Is an object such as an artificial womb so different, or is it just the logical advancement in the history of these technologies? Humans adapt to new technologies—whereas cryptocurrency or even credit cards were once met with skepticism by people who could not imagine an immaterial form of cash, these forms are now widely used and accepted. Could we similarly adapt to babies being born from artificial wombs or even from humanoid robots? Or is something lost when birth ceases to be a human activity, and if so, what is it that we are losing?

Artificial womb technology, also known as ectogenesis, dates to 1954, when an inventor named Emanuel Greenberg filed the first patent for an artificial uterus (see figure below). As science writer Tom Ireland has described in his 2024 article “To Be Born in a Bag,” the ethics of early experimentation with this technology would be difficult to grasp for those in the modern world. Ireland cites early research using Greenberg’s artificial uterus, for example, that involved keeping aborted human fetuses alive for several hours during experimentation with the contraption. Since that time, those creating artificial wombs have primarily focused on how to temporarily assist a premature infant during key developmental phases of gestation, though others have worked to create a device that could replicate the womb, pregnancy, and birth.

Our technology in these matters is not yet at the point of Brave New World, but artificial wombs are quickly developing past the purpose of supporting premature babies, catapulting us all closer to a future in which human babies could be conceived, grown and born entirely from outside the human body.


Figure 1: Early artificial womb design, 1954 patent application submitted by Emanuel M. Greenberg.Credit: U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (also in Tom Ireland, “To Be Born in a Bag,” 2024).

Recent data from the World Health Organization estimates that approximately 15 million infants are delivered prematurely each year globally, and complications arising from premature birth claim the lives of around one million of those infants annually. In response to these statistics, research teams across multiple countries have been working to develop artificial wombs capable of supporting preterm infants through the most vulnerable phase of neonatal development, which is the period prior to 28 weeks of gestation. The infant incubator, which dates to an 1835 warming device invented by physician Johann Georg von Ruehl, was first used to help premature babies survive an early birth. Since then, many research teams, including those at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands, the EXTrauterine Environment of Neonatal Development (EXTEND) program at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), and the Ex-Vivo Uterine Environment (EVE) program at Tohoku University in Japan have started working in this field, indicating a growing urgency and international scope to how artificial wombs are developing.

The main concern driving all these projects is that conventional incubators, which introduce air into the infant’s lungs, pose serious risks to preterm babies. The respiratory systems of these babies are not yet developed enough to handle this. Once an infant reaches the 28-week threshold, the risks associated with premature birth diminish substantially, and the infant can be transitioned from the artificial womb into a standard neonatal care unit. The approach being pursued at Eindhoven includes immersing preterm infants in fluid-filled, bag-like enclosures connected to an artificial placenta. This system is designed to replicate the conditions of the natural uterine environment as closely as possible.

Of all the groups currently active in the field, the CHOP team’s EXTEND program remains closest to human clinical trials, having entered direct discussions with the United States Food and Drug Administration for the first in-human testing. Taken together, these efforts suggest that artificial womb technology is transitioning from smaller national programs into a coordinated international research priority. Human trials are potentially on the near horizon.

Ireland explains that researchers working in this field generally find it absurd to think that a womb could be replicated to the point of growing an embryo or fetus completely outside of a mother’s body. However, he makes note of companies such as Colossal Biosciences, a group devoted to using DNA from ancient woolly mammoths to create a living mammoth, grown in an artificial womb, by 2027. Using this type of technology to recreate an ancient creature from conception is a slippery slope to using it to create human beings from scratch, just like using CRISPR gene editing technology to protect humans from harmful genetic mutations could open the door to using it for less ethical purposes, such as creating “designer babies.”

There are more speculative projects envisioning a future with artificial womb technology. One of these is the EctoLife project, a concept render depicting the world’s first artificial womb facility. It is created by Hashem Al-Ghaili, a filmmaker and self-proclaimed biotechnologist and science communicator. Among the scenarios it is designed to address are biological conception for infertile couples, the elimination of premature birth and cesarean delivery, a means of boosting birth rates in countries experiencing population decline, and the removal of the physical pain associated with childbirth for women. In an attempt to emulate human embodiment, Al-Ghaili even envisions a haptic suit transmitting the physical sensations of fetal movement such as prenatal kicks and rolls to the wearer as the fetus develops within the pod.

Artificial womb technology, in both its current and projected forms, has the potential to fundamentally transform our collective understanding of what it means for a child to be born from a woman’s body or even a human body. Should such technologies develop to their full potential, we will need to renegotiate what it means to be born or give birth—the social implications of which remain an open question.

To understand why this renegotiation is so significant, it is helpful to situate ectogenesis within a longer trajectory of reproductive technologies that have already resulted in shifts to our collective understanding of conception, pregnancy, and parenthood. In philosophy, the field of social ontology looks at how humans construct the social world and create meaning. New practices, technologies, and forms of human cooperation can in some cases coalesce to generate new institutional facts and transform or even displace old ones. The emergence of cryptocurrency, to use the non-reproductive example mentioned earlier, has already begun to reshape the collective intentionality that underlies our understanding of what money is and how it functions. Reproductive technology is undergoing its own similar evolution.

The advent of in vitro fertilization severed the link between sexual intercourse and conception, allowing for the possibility that a child could be conceived without any sexual contact between its biological parents. Surrogacy further transformed this reproductive chain by separating biological gestation from biological parenthood—suddenly, a child could be carried to term in a body genetically unrelated to it. Each of these developments has required and gradually received a reconstitution of collective intentionality (from John Searle’s philosophy on social ontology, “collective intentionality” is a unified mental consensus that percolates within a group of people, impacting how they understand and develop the beliefs, goals, objects, and rules that form the bedrock of society): new institutional facts emerge and new legal frameworks are constructed. IVF-conceived children are recognized without question as fully “born,” for example, and children carried by surrogates are legally and socially incorporated as the children of their intended parents.

SUGGESTED READING The radical future of humanity without childbirth By Claire Horn

What is striking is that the predicted endpoint of this trajectory, which is the complete removal of sexual intercourse from the reproductive process, was foreseen at the very moment ectogenesis was first named. Biologist J.B.S. Haldane, who coined the term “ectogenesis,” explicitly argued in his 1924 book Daedalus or Science and the Futurethat the technology would enable what he called the separation of sexual love and reproduction. For Haldane, this was a utopian prospect. His friend Aldous Huxley took a much darker and dystopian view: in his 1932 novel Brave New World, all reproduction takes place within the Central London Hatchery and Conditioning Centre, entirely without sexual intercourse. Nearly a century later, the question is no longer whether such a separation is conceivable, but what it would mean for the meaning of birth (birth’s social ontology) if it were to become normalized.

Birth is not merely a biological event; it is also an institutional fact, constituted by the intersection of collective agreement and social function with the biological event. A child is recognized as “born” not simply because it has emerged from a gestational environment, but because a web of collective understandings, communal and social recognitions, and legal declarations marks that status. There is a collective, social agreement that a woman should be called a mother and treated differently after she gives birth, for example. Institutional facts arise from that agreement, such as that a mother should receive certain forms of care and treatment following the birth of her child, or time off from work.

What concerns me most about ectogenesis and the meaning of birth is the extent to which birth from the human body is profoundly valuable on aesthetic and existential levels. A possible world in which birth from the body disappears altogether would also mean the loss of a quintessentially sublime and interconnected experience between two beings—a mother (or birth giver) and child.

In Western philosophy, the sublime has long been a topic of interest to the field of aesthetics, finding a particularly fruitful point of emergence during the Age of the Enlightenment. It was at this time that philosophers such as Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) and Edmund Burke (1729-1797) in Europe became interested in our inability to fully grasp the concept of greatness as it exists in nature and the human experience. Philosopher Sheila Lintott has described these conceptions as “masculinist”—not because the philosophers were men, but because they focused their approach to the sublime on mental, emotional, and psychological strength, as opposed to experiences of embodiment, which would include birth—a predominantly female experience. Kant’s “masculinist” focus is also present, claims Lintott, in how he diminishes women more broadly, and in particular, their ability at experiencing the sublime when he suggests that women require male guidance in intellectual matters. Turning her focus from experiences of the sublime in nature, Lintott developed a theory of the sublime in a feminine context over a decade ago: the sublime is an embodied experience for those who give birth—this experience is visceral and involves bodily strength and physical sensations, as well as psychological fears. In the context of pregnancy, Lintott describes the sublime as a complex experience during which time pregnant women may encounter both positive and negative psychological states, including those even of dread.

Political theorist Iris Marion Young famously wrote about the “doubling of the pregnant subject,” which refers to the way that those who are pregnant experience their own bodies and the other body within them. Lintott takes this issue of embodying another body as part of the sublime in gestation, and particularly the greatness or magnitude felt by those who are pregnant when they both contemplate and feel the way in which one body is enveloped within another during pregnancy. The pregnant self is never entirely one person nor two; it exists in a liminal space between two beings. Philosopher Jonna Bornemark gives her own description of this doubling of the pregnant self, explaining phenomena such as a pregnant woman being touched and touching that which is touching her from within, for example, and how this experience is one not just of her own body but of the body within the body.

While the many physiological transformations that those who are pregnant undergo are fascinating on a scientific or observational level, there is also an aesthetic dimension to the experience of being pregnant. Feeling a fluttering in one’s womb for the first time, for example, which occurs when fetal movement takes place in the uterus and usually begins during the second trimester of pregnancy, is a phenomenon known as “quickening.” This experience has a quality of sensation unlike any other in the human experience. Some have described it as the sensation of a butterfly’s wings fluttering and delicately touching the internal sides of the womb. Braxton Hicks contractions, known as false or practice contractions, felt during the second and third trimesters, also have a unique aesthetic quality to them, bringing the attention of those who are pregnant to a tightening of the uterus. In the case of my own two pregnancies, this tightening felt almost as if a thick invisible band were simultaneously pressing and pushing my womb, but in a rhythmic way, similar to how I imagine the pressure between tectonic plates growing and releasing as the earth’s plates shift.

Those who have experienced these bodily sensations may have encountered the sublime. Similarly, other fetal motion experienced during pregnancy, which can include kicks, jabs, and rolls, can be simultaneously exhilarating and frightening. In some cases, often captured in photography, the fetus’ foot or hand pushes strongly against the uterus, showing its impression on the outside of the pregnant woman’s belly. This visible marker of the internal body contained within the pregnant body is both felt through sensation and experienced emotionally, sometimes even by partners who bear witness to this event or feel the kicks themselves.

We need to realize what it is about human gestation that matters, and at the rate that artificial womb technology is developing, we should do so fast.

These events are both typical and extraordinary in pregnancy, and they also play a part in prenatal bonding between mother and child. Research in pre- and perinatal psychology, as well as in psychiatry, has shown us that an offspring’s brain development in utero can be affected by the pregnant mother’s experiences, as well as by these moments of bonding that take place during pregnancy.These moments of bonding are not one-sided; research suggests that a mother’s experiences during pregnancy can affect fetal brain development, hinting at a form of communication between the two that we are only beginning to understand. Experiences of the sublime could be shared on some level between the mother and the fetus during pregnancy.

The act of giving birth can take many forms, especially in the modern world where technological and medical intervention is common. Yet in all those forms there is an aesthetic quality to the experience of giving birth. In the case of an unmedicated birth, the physical act of the newborn crowning coincides with an aesthetic experience of the mother found both in the sensation of feeling a baby emerge from one’s body as well as in what may amount to a multitude of emotions experienced by the birth giver releasing a new being into the world. This experience is physical, but it is also intellectual and emotional. Part of maternal subjectivity is emotional, and these emotions are intimately bound to the aesthetics of embodiment—pregnant subjects both physically feel the changes and processes of their transformed bodies and experience thoughts and emotions related to those feelings.

If artificial womb technology develops to the point where it replaces human pregnancy and birth, the aesthetics of all these experiences—the quality of birth and of being born, as well as the complex interaction of prenatal communication—will be lost. A fetus’ kicks and movements are early forms of communication, often met with a touch or movement from pregnant mothers or their partners. The act of birth is a physiological internal journey for both the mother and child, the end result of which is unity between the two entities on the outside of the body. Some pre- and perinatal psychologists have suggested that these experiences in fact affect the psychology of both beings, having an impact on their future well-being, and in the case of the newborn child, on its development later in life.

There are ways of trying to reproduce the prenatal womb in an artificial way: isolettes containing large holes on their sides allow parents to reach in and touch the baby. However, most parents and doctors would agree that while helpful, this experience is not the same as, nor as beneficial for either the baby or the parent, as would be carrying the baby to term. Incubators were developed for the emergency situations of preterm infants, not for the purpose of growing babies.

In her recent book on ectogenesis and the value of human experience, humanities scholar Laura Johnson Dahlke provides her readers with several childbirth narratives coming from different women, all of which describe different aspects of what it is to experience awe in giving birth. Maternal awe, she argues, is an integral foundation of the human species. Ectogenetic technology would not only remove this experience of awe but would also interfere with this foundational aspect of who we are as a species. As humanities professor Agnes Howard says in her review of Dahlke’s book, we need to realize what it is about human gestation that matters, and at the rate that artificial womb technology is developing, we should do so fast.

Ultimately, while we cannot discern exactly what advanced technology around ectogenesis would mean for the human experience, we can be sure that both the ritual of birth and the aesthetics of birth, including experiences of the sublime, would be interrupted or lost. It is also highly improbable that the bonding which takes place between mothers and fetuses during the prenatal period could ever be replicated by a machine. It should be said in closing that adoption is a beautiful and legitimate path to parenthood, and nothing argued here is meant to suggest otherwise. The question specifically is what would be lost to humanity if pregnancy and birth from the body were no longer part of our world. Pregnancy and birth are journeys shared by the mother (or birth giver) and child. Even if a child is later adopted, those journeys do matter. As prenatal psychology and studies on intergenerational trauma that begins in the womb tell us, these journeys and experiences of prenatal bonding can impact a child’s wellbeing into the future. The journey into the world through a connection to the maternal body matters, and it is something that will disappear if ectogenesis replaces human birth.
